title: The General Paradigm: Three Fundamental Aspects

reading.text: Self-contained lesson. Optional background: Goldreich's Primer, Ch. 1 (the general paradigm)

body:
## The general paradigm: one framework, many generators

The study of pseudorandom generators is part of complexity theory, and the Primer advocates a **unified view** of all its notions.
Every concrete notion of a pseudorandom generator is an incarnation of one abstract paradigm: a deterministic algorithm that stretches a short random seed into a longer output sequence.
A generic formulation consists of specifying **three fundamental aspects**.

### 1. The stretch measure

The generator is a **deterministic algorithm** that stretches k-bit long seeds into `ℓ(k)`-bit long outputs, where the **stretch function** satisfies **`ℓ(k) > k`** for all k.
The function `ℓ: ℕ → ℕ` is called the stretch measure (or stretch function) of the generator.
Larger ℓ is more useful, but in some settings the specific measure is immaterial, since stretch can be amplified.
Note that the output length cannot exceed the generator's running time, so ℓ is polynomially bounded.

### 2. The class of distinguishers

The generator must “fool” some non-trivial class of algorithms: any algorithm from a predetermined class D cannot distinguish the generator's output (on a uniform seed) from a uniformly chosen sequence.
Formally, for any distinguisher D ∈ D, any threshold function f ∈ F, and all sufficiently large k:

$$|\Pr[D(G(U_k)){=}1] - \Pr[D(U_{\ell(k)}){=}1]| < f(k)$$

where the class F of threshold functions determines which differences count as **noticeable**.
The archetypical choice is D = all probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms and F = reciprocals of positive polynomials.
A distinguisher is an observer that tries to tell whether the tested string is G(U_k) or a truly random string U_{ℓ(k)}; the condition requires D's verdict to be the same in both cases, up to a negligible difference.

### 3. The resources of the generator

The third aspect is the **computational complexity of the generator itself**, viewed as an algorithm.
The archetypical choice: the generator works in polynomial time (polynomial in the length of its input — the seed).
Placing no computational requirements on the generator yields “generators” that can even fool any subexponential-size circuit family.

## Some instantiations of the paradigm 

The rest of the course is a map of the paradigm. Two important instantiations relate to polynomial-time distinguishers:

- **General-purpose pseudorandom generators (Chapter 2):** the generator runs in polynomial time and must withstand **any probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher**, including ones that run for more time than the generator itself.
The same generator can be used safely in any efficient application.
- **Generators for derandomization (Chapter 3):** the generator may run **more time than the distinguisher**, which is viewed as a fixed circuit of size bounded by a fixed polynomial.
This relaxed relation is what makes full derandomization results (e.g., BPP = P under suitable assumptions) possible.

Two further families focus on the type of the distinguisher rather than its time bound:

- **Space-bounded generators (Chapter 4):** the potential distinguishers are space-bounded computations, and the aspects are fixed by the space-complexity of the distinguisher and the generator.
- **Special-purpose generators (Chapter 5):** the generator only needs to exhibit limited random behavior — e.g., pair-wise independence, small bias, or hitting frequency — and such generators can be constructed **without any computational complexity assumption**.

## Why the paradigm matters

Every definition in this course is obtained by fixing the three aspects; disagreements about “what is a pseudorandom generator” are really disagreements about the choices in @def:paradigm
Keep this framework in your pocket: when you meet a new generator, ask (1) what does it stretch and how far? (2) whom must it fool? (3) how much computation may it spend?
The four families above — general-purpose, derandomization, space-bounded, special-purpose — are the itinerary of Chapters 2–5.

defs.name: The general paradigm of pseudorandom generators
defs.statement: A generic formulation of pseudorandom generators consists of three fundamental aspects: the stretch measure (a function ℓ(k) > k), the class of distinguishers to fool, and the resources the generator is allowed to use.
defs.intuition: Every notion of a pseudorandom generator is an instantiation of these three choices.

checkpoints.question: Which triple of choices instantiates the general paradigm as a *general-purpose* pseudorandom generator?

options.text: Stretch ℓ(k) > k; distinguishers = all probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms; generator = fixed polynomial-time.
Stretch ℓ(k) = k; distinguishers = space-bounded algorithms; generator = exponential-time.
Stretch ℓ(k) > k; distinguishers = fixed-size circuits; generator = polynomial-time.
Stretch ℓ(k) > k; distinguishers = polynomial-time algorithms; generator = no complexity bound.

checkpoints.explanation: By §1.4.3, general-purpose generators correspond to the case where the generator itself runs in (fixed) polynomial time and must withstand any probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher, including distinguishers that run for more time than the generator; the stretch function only needs to satisfy ℓ(k) > k. The derandomization instantiation, in contrast, lets the generator run more time than a fixed-size-circuit distinguisher (M1-2 in COURSE.md §4).

exercises.prompt: Fill in the framework: for each of the four instantiations listed in §1.4.3 (general-purpose, derandomization, space-bounded, special-purpose), state the choice for each of the three fundamental aspects.
exercises.hint: Start from §1.4.3's two polynomial-time-distinguisher instantiations; the key contrast is who may be more complex — the generator or the distinguisher.
